title: Four Paper Cups in the Back Right Corner
teaser: The wedding order is due at 11:30, but the first tray of cupcakes comes out progressively darker from the front left to the back right. The recipe, portion size, and baking time have not changed, so Xiao Qiao first has to find out whether the difference follows the batter or the position in the oven.
paragraphs: At 8:40 in the morning, the bakery had to finish ninety-six wedding cupcakes by 11:30, but the first test tray of twenty-four had gone wrong. The row at the front left was pale, the cakes grew darker toward the back right, and the four in the far corner were close to overbaked. Xiao Qiao had made the same recipe the night before. That morning she had weighed thirty-five grams of batter into every cavity, the oven display had stayed at 180 degrees, and the timer had sounded exactly at sixteen minutes. The head baker was in the front shop rushing another order and only told her not to put the second tray into the oven yet. He did not tell her what the problem was.

Xiao Qiao first thought of lowering the oven temperature by ten degrees across the board. But after unmoulding the cakes, she placed them back on the table in the same six-by-four arrangement they had occupied on the tray. The color difference was not scattered at random. It formed a clear gradient from the front left to the back right. If the whole oven were simply too hot, the cakes at the front left should not still be pale. If a few portions of batter had been weighed incorrectly, the color should not change continuously with position. She took four thirty-gram portions from the remaining batter, put them into four identical paper cups marked A, B, C, and D on the bottom, and placed one at each corner of the tray. She baked them for only eight minutes. When they came out, D in the back right was the darkest, while A in the front left was the palest.

She did not treat “D burns more easily” as an answer. For the second test she again used four thirty-gram portions, but placed cup A in the back-right corner and D in the front-left corner, switching the other two as well. Eight minutes later, A had become the darkest, while D was now the palest. On the back of the order card, Xiao Qiao drew a small rectangle and marked a circle in the back-right corner. The result shifted her attention away from the recipe and the cups and toward the inside of the oven: at least over that period, the back-right area was delivering more heat.

Knowing that “the back right is hotter” was still not enough. The ninety-six finished cakes had to meet the same standard for doneness and color. Xiao Qiao made only four small samples for a third test. She left the tray in its original position for four minutes, turned it 180 degrees when the timer sounded, and baked for another four. The four samples came out much closer in color. She cut two open as well; both centers were fully set, so the appearance had not been improved by simply underbaking them. On the first full tray for the wedding order, she therefore kept the oven at 180 degrees and the total time at sixteen minutes, but rotated the tray at the eight-minute mark. All twenty-four cakes were baked through. The cakes from the right rear were still slightly darker, but the obvious gradient from the first tray had disappeared.

That new result led her to make one more adjustment. Starting with the second production tray, she placed the decorated designs that needed the most visual consistency toward the middle and moved the rotation point forward to the seventh minute. She used the same arrangement for the third and fourth trays. At 10:58, all ninety-six finished cakes were out of the oven. When the head baker returned, he first broke one open to check the center, then picked up the lightest and darkest cakes from the same tray and held them side by side. Finally he rolled the cooling rack over to the packing table. No one counted the first test tray as part of the wedding order. Those cakes stayed behind for samples in the shop.

At 11:24, the customer arrived to collect the order. Xiao Qiao crossed out the red circle on the order card. While clearing the station, she noticed the four paper cups still lined up beside the sink. The rim of A was darker than D, but only because A had spent the second test in the back-right corner. She stacked the four cups together and slipped them, along with the order card bearing the little rectangle, into the flour-dusted logbook beside the oven. One corner of the paper remained visible, with a black dot at its edge.
concept: Kolb’s experiential learning cycle describes how experience can be turned into learning. A concrete experience first produces an observable result. The learner then looks back, compares what happened, forms a working explanation or hypothesis that can account for the difference, and tests it through purposeful action. The result of that test becomes a new concrete experience and begins another cycle. The point is not that “doing something more often naturally makes you good at it,” but that experience, reflection, explanation, and experimentation form a loop that can continue to be revised.
explanation: The color gradient on the first tray is the concrete experience. Xiao Qiao does not simply repeat the bake or blame a general problem such as “the oven is too hot.” She reconstructs where the cakes sat on the tray and observes the gradient. She then uses two four-cup tests to distinguish between “something is wrong with a particular portion of batter or cup” and “different positions in the oven receive different heat.” After A and D switch places, the darker result follows the back-right position rather than the letter, supporting the explanation that this part of the oven is hotter. A third test—rotating the tray—then directly tests a response while preserving the standard for doneness. The full production batch creates further evidence, which leads to another adjustment on the next tray instead of turning the first explanation into a permanent answer.
mapping: The first twenty-four cakes form a color gradient from the front left to the back right → A concrete experience produces a result that does not match the expected process.

The cakes are restored to their original positions and compared against portion size, time, and color distribution → Reflective observation breaks “the batch went wrong” into differences that can be examined.

After A and D switch positions, the darker result still appears in the oven’s back-right corner → A discriminating test supports the working explanation that the heat differs by position rather than reflecting a random guess.

The tray is rotated at eight minutes and doneness is checked, then the rotation is moved to seven minutes based on the production result → Active experimentation creates new experience, and the new experience continues to refine later action.
boundary: Kolb’s cycle does not require real learning to move neatly through four separate stages. Observation, interpretation, and experimentation often overlap or loop back, and they may draw on prior knowledge or other people’s experience. One small test also cannot prove that the oven’s back-right corner will always run hotter. Where food safety, equipment failure, or other high-risk operations are involved, experiential testing must remain within professional rules and required checks; “learning by doing” cannot replace safety standards.
reflection: If Xiao Qiao had simply lowered the temperature by ten degrees and happened to produce one tray with the right color, what would she actually have learned, and what would still be impossible to judge on the next tray?
